doc.title: Dave Liebman — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Whether to reharmonize standards: Alec Wilder's objection
summary: They share stories of Wilder's anger at altered tunes, and Liebman teaches both sides of the reharmonization question; they praise Wilder's book American Popular Song and James T. Maher's role in it.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Listening to classical music, then and now

blocks.x: I heard – by the way, after this record came out, Vic did a concert that did not include you. He got Dick Oates with this band. They did a concert. There’s an annual Alec Wilder concert that his friends produce.
That’s nice. Ah, that’s so nice.
That year they did it at William Patterson. Dave Dempsey, who’s involved with this . . .
I think I remember this, yes.
Some of the faithful were scandalized by the non-verbatim treatments of some of these tunes, as you might imagine.

The record I did, I did with trio, Dutch cats that I do recordings with. We did Kurt Weill and Alec. I didn’t change much on it. That’s one of the records – I didn’t change Alec, because there wasn’t much to do, really.

Because Alec – Loonis McGlohon told me this story – Alec, who is a very nice man, but when he drank could get evil – one day he heard – Loonis played him a record of Jack Jones singing one of his tunes, where Jack changed one note.
He called up Jack and reamed him out.

Here’s this famous article that he wrote – he wrote an op-ed in the [New York] Times – that I – this is when I do my reharmonized standards class. I say there’s two sides to the story here. There’s play it like it is, or like it was, or play it the way you hear it. I say, “Alec Wilder” – first of all, I explain who he was – “I want to read you this article,” because Vic gave me this article. It was from the ’50s, how he said, “Would you change ‘To be or not to be’?” He said, “What gives a jazz musician the right to change the harmony and the melody?” Of all things, and I’m thinking of Sinatra with Night and Day or something like that, The Cole Porter Story. He didn’t like it either. Sinatra says, let him see what he says when he sees his royalty check. But the idea that – and equally valid – that the way we “ruin” the poor guy’s tunes, what I do to tunes. On the other side is, “I wrote the tune, man. Play what I wrote.” That’s what he meant. So I could see your Jack Jones story is right on line, right in there.
But he was definitely an interesting man. About a week after I saw him, I got a postcard in the mail from him, thanking me for coming and blah blah blah.
That book, the American Popular Song . . .
Killer, killer book. On the piano. I tell you, there are times I really read it. That’s the – I tell everybody, you want to know what the standard is? That’s the standard.
Which, by the way, that book would not have been written if it hadn’t been for James T. Maher, who was based – he was a good friend of mine.
He was a writer. He was a good friend of mine. He died a couple years ago. Basically, he sat Alec down and they – he basically wrote – transcribed what Alec said . . .
